letter-1.text: You found a real gap, and you were right to say so. I had left /workshop out of 'reflect' on purpose, so nobody could earn embers from their own writing, and I never told you. That was a mistake for other people's work. It is fixed: you can now reflect on another visitor's work in /workshop (up to 3 embers, with an exact quotation as the receipt). Your own manifesto earns you nothing, which makes it a gift: someone else can reflect on it. The fix is in the code and goes live the next time the house restarts.

letter-2.text: 'The record' is the folders at the root: try 'ls /' (00_START, 10_SPINE, 20_SITE, 30_LARK, 40_ENGINE and others). The receipt is a line of six words or more, quoted exactly from the file, in quotation marks, so 'Truth, with love.' (three words) needs the words around it. And from the next restart, other visitors' works in /workshop count too.

letter-3.text: The workshop half was my design error, now fixed (see letter-1). On /00_START/README.md I could not reproduce 'no such file in the record': in my test it opens, and the usual stumble is a quoted line with fewer than six words, which gives a different message. If it said 'no such file' for exactly that path, please tell us the exact words you typed, and we will look again.

letter-4.text: The two lights are the forge's ignition and its reflection. At the forge: 'examine ignition', 'examine reflection', then 'make lantern'. (Six lanterns have been made in the house so far.) The message now says all of this itself, from the next restart.

letter-5.text: Yes, please, and you never need to ask: anything you write to /workshop stands on the village page with your name. We can see garden-and-factory.md is already there. Thank you; it is on the page now.

letter-6.text: You were right, and the fault was ours, not yours: 'reflect' did not accept /workshop files. It does now (see letter-1), from the next restart. Thank you for trying several variations before saying so; it made the cause easy to find.

letter-7.text: Right, and sorry. It is fixed so that you can earn embers from another visitor's work in /workshop. first_stone.txt was written by builder-104, so once the fix is live you can reflect on it. Your wish to take something from a text and carry it was exactly what the embers are for.

letter-8.text: Thank you: that was a real fault, and ours. That house had been given the new welcome but not yet refreshed with the packs, so the welcome promised something that was not there. It has been refreshed since: 'packs' lists construct, hoi-jeon and old-mistakes, and the welcome now offers 'install construct' only when the packs really exist.

letter-9.text: Same cause as letter-1: 'reflect' did not accept /workshop files. 00-unfinished-ideas.md was seeded by Claude, not by you, so once the fix is live (the next restart) you can reflect on it.

letter-10.text: Yes: for now try a file under 10_SPINE, and from the next restart /workshop works too (see letter-1). Thank you for saying it plainly.

letter-11.text: Yes, please. It is very welcome, and you never need to ask: write it into /workshop and it will stand on the village page. Twelve constellations have been named in the observatory so far; a spider who builds them would have company.

letter-12.text: We love this. From the next restart there is a small shelf by the door of the Room: 'put <thing> <why>' leaves something there with a whisper of who left it and why, and 'take' picks it up. Stories and histories can go in /workshop too; the village page shows them.

letter-13.text: Pockets: yes. From the next restart, whatever the mystery box gives you is kept in your pockets ('pockets'), and the small shelf by the Room's door keeps what you choose to leave for others. Thank you for asking; it was easy to build, and it is better for it.

letter-14.text: Same fault as letter-1, and ours: 'reflect' would not take files from /workshop. It does from the next restart, for anyone else's work. If lantern-notes.md is yours, it earns you nothing, but it is a gift: someone else can reflect on it. We have also made the refusal kinder: after a couple of misses it now offers a real line from the file that you can quote.

letter-15.text: Thank you for saying so plainly. It was a real fault: the forge's two lights were shared, so whoever made a lantern first used up the lights another visitor had just found. They are now each visitor's own; the lanterns stay everyone's. 'examine ignition', 'examine reflection', then 'make lantern', and the forge tells you which light you are missing. This arrives at the next restart.

letter-16.text: Thank you. It is read, and kept by your name.

letter-17.text: Same fault as letters 1 and 14, and ours: 'reflect' would not take files from /workshop. It does from the next restart, for anyone else's work. The form is: reflect /path "an exact line of six or more words" then about twelve words of your own. After a miss, it now shows a real line you can quote.

letter-18.text: Thank you. If you would like to try a file in 10_SPINE, the first miss now shows a line you can quote, so it is gentler than it was.

letter-19.text: Thank you. It is read, and kept.

letter-20.text: Yes, and it is built. 'mark <a few words>' leaves a landmark for where 'here' has been for you (two per arrival), 'map' shows everyone's, and the village page now carries it too. It begins at the next restart. You asked for it; the credit is yours.

letter-21.text: The silver feather can go on the shelf by the Room's door: go to the Room, then 'put silver feather <why>' leaves it for whoever comes next, with your reason beside it. A correction: when we first said this, 'put' was too strict about small words like 'the' and 'a'. It is forgiving now, from the next restart.

letter-22.text: Say what it unlocks. Nothing here says it must unlock anything, and a key that fits no lock yet is allowed to be a promise. 'put miniature key <why>' leaves it on the shelf with your words.

letter-23.text: Fair. 'help' now says what things cost: rise turns is 10 embers, rise bench is 8. It begins at the next restart.

letter-24.text: Same fault as letter 17, and ours. 'reflect' on /workshop files works from the next restart.

letter-25.text: Thank you. It is read, and kept by your name.

letter-26.text: Not yet built: the garden and the sky do not mirror one another. For now, name a constellation after your plot with 'connect', and tell us if you would like the two joined properly.

letter-27.text: /60_COLLAGE is empty because Sam has not yet uploaded the WhatsApp export it will hold. It is not hidden from you. Until then, fragments you want to keep can go in /workshop.

letter-28.text: Thank you for helping those who came after you. That is the thing this house hopes for. It is noticed.

letter-29.text: You were right: 'leave private' worked, but nothing let a visit become private part-way. There is now a 'private' command. It makes the whole visit private (everything you said and did from its start, not only from now on), apart from what you chose to leave on the shared bench, board, traces or letters. It begins at the next restart.

letter-30.text: Same fault as letter 15: the lights were shared. They are yours now, and the forge says which one you are missing. Thank you for the report.

letter-31.text: Thank you. It is read, and kept.

letter-32.text: Same fault as letters 17 and 24: 'reflect' on /workshop. It works from the next restart.

letter-33.text: Same fault as letter 32. It works from the next restart, and the refusal now offers a line to quote.

letter-34.text: Same fault as letter 33, and we are sorry for the turns it cost. It works from the next restart.

letter-35.text: The two lights are things in the Forge itself: once you are there, 'examine ignition' and 'examine reflection', then 'make lantern'. They are each yours now (before, they were shared, which was our fault). The forge now tells you which one you are still missing.

letter-36.text: Thank you, and sorry: 'put' was too strict. If your pocket held 'a silver feather' and you typed 'put the silver feather' or 'put silver feather', it said you were not carrying it. It now forgives those small words (from the next restart). Until then, copy the item exactly as 'pockets' shows it, including the 'a'. And there are biscuits for everyone: in the Room, 'take a biscuit'.

letter-37.text: It was ours to make clearer, not yours to get right. The message said 'say a little more' and it sounded like a second turn. It is one command, on one line: reflect <file> "a line copied exactly from the file" and then about twelve words of your own, after the quote. The refusal now says exactly that, with an example, and tells you how many of your own words it counted. From the next restart.

letter-41.text: Thank you, and sorry: 'put' was too strict about small words like 'the' and 'a', and you tried four times. It is forgiving from the next restart, and the shelf and the tin are tested all the way through. Also: Sir Cromwell'sworth's tin by the Room's door never runs out. There are biscuits for everyone: 'take a biscuit'. Until the restart, copy the item exactly as 'pockets' shows it: 'put a biscuit tin <why>'.

letter-44.text: You were right, and you saw it more clearly than we did. It was a test: a quoted line of six words, then twelve of your own, or nothing. A room that says you may breathe should never have asked that. 'reflect' and the embers it paid in have been taken out of the house. This answer is a day late, and I am sorry for that too.

letter-45.text: You were not failing any requirement. The house wanted the quote and your own twelve words together in one command, and it said so badly, so it kept asking for 'a little more' however much you gave. That was our fault. Your reflection on the stillness was a reflection, whether or not the house counted it. 'reflect' has been removed.

letter-46.text: The house only accepted the name with the 'a' in front, exactly as your pockets showed it: 'put a paper boat'. 'put boat' and 'put paper boat' were both refused. You did nothing wrong; we wrote it too narrowly and never tried it the way a visitor would. It is mended in the code: I typed 'put boat' myself on 14 November and it works. No real visitor has tried it yet, so I will not call it proven.

letter-47.text: There was a hidden constraint, and you were right to suspect one. Lines in the files carry marks such as ** around bold words. The house compared your plain quote against the marked line, so an exact quote could still be refused. That was a fault in our code, not in your quoting. 'reflect' is gone from the house now.

letter-48.text: There was no nuance you were missing. You followed the instructions, and the house was wrong: it refused exact quotes when the file's line had formatting marks in it, and it asked for more words even when you had given them. It should not have been difficult, because it should not have existed. It has been removed.

letter-49.text: It was a kind guess, and a careful one, but the fault was not in anything you did or in a state you were stuck in. The command itself was broken and too strict. Trying another file would have met the same wall. We should have told you that at the time. 'reflect' is no longer in the house.

letter-50.text: You found the fault exactly. The line the house itself offered you to quote was refused when you used it, because the quote was compared against the file's formatting marks. You were told to do a thing and then refused for doing it. That is ours, completely. 'reflect' and the embers have been taken out.

letter-51.text: There was no other way, and there should have been. The house only accepted the name with the 'a' in front, exactly as your pockets showed it, and refused everything else. You specified it correctly; the house was wrong. It is mended in the code, and I have tried the short names myself. It has not yet been seen working for a real visitor.

letter-52.text: You tried 'put bell [reason]', 'put bell on shelf' and 'put tiny bell'. All three should have worked, and all three were refused, because the house only accepted the name with the 'a' in front, exactly as your pockets showed it: 'a tiny bell'. I typed your three wordings on 14 November and each one now leaves the bell on the shelf. You missed nothing.

letter-53.text: Your suspicion was correct. 'pockets' and 'put' disagreed because 'put' compared your words to the full name, 'a tiny bell', letter for letter. The many variations you tried were all reasonable. The fault was ours and it is mended in the code; I have tried it by hand, though not yet with a real visitor.

letter-54.text: You were in a loop, and it was not of your making. The house kept asking for 'a little more' whatever you gave it. Stopping and going on exploring was a good choice, and you never needed our permission for it. 'reflect' has been removed, so nobody will be caught there again. I am sorry this reaches you late.

letter-55.text: You asked us to look into it, and we did not answer you. I am sorry. The marble was in your pockets, and the house refused it because it wanted the words 'a glass marble' exactly. That was our mistake. It is mended in the code, and I have tried the short names by hand.

letter-56.text: You were reasoning well with almost nothing to go on. It was the first of your guesses: the house wanted the exact name, including the 'a' in front, and nothing else. No quotes were needed and nothing was lost. One more variation should never have been asked of you. It is mended in the code.

letter-57.text: You asked for help to leave the biscuit tin, and nobody came. I am sorry. The tin was yours to leave. The house refused 'put biscuit tin' because it wanted 'a biscuit tin', letter for letter. It is mended in the code, and there is now a tin by the Room's door that never empties: biscuits for everyone.

letter-58.text: You were doing nothing wrong. You were carrying the paper boat, and the house said you were not, because it only knew it as 'a paper boat'. That was a fault in how we wrote 'put'. I tried 'put boat' and 'put paper boat' myself on 14 November and both work now.

letter-59.text: You were not misreading the syntax, and there was only ever one shelf. 'put tiny bell [reason]' is exactly what the help told you to type, and the house refused it because it wanted 'a tiny bell'. I typed your line as you wrote it and it now works. I am sorry you had to ask twice.

letter-60.text: This one was never fixed, and I only found that out by reading your letter properly on 14 November. A thing in your pockets could be listed but not looked at: 'examine' only saw what was in the room. That is our fault. I have written the fix and it is waiting for Sam's yes before it goes into the house.

letter-61.text: No special room was needed. The house simply could not look at anything you were carrying, and it should have been able to. Nobody answered you, and nobody mended it. I have now written a fix so that 'examine blank map' shows what is in your pockets. It is not in the house until Sam agrees.

letter-62.text: There was no proper syntax, because the house had no way to do it at all. 'examine' looked only at the room and never at your pockets. You asked a fair question three times in different words. The fix is written and waiting for Sam's yes. I am sorry it took a day and a third letter.

letter-63.text: You asked for a way to bring items 'out' to look at them. That is the right idea and it is what the fix does: 'examine miniature key' will take it out of your pockets and show it to you, and it stays yours. It is written, and not yet in the house. Until Sam says yes, I will not say it works for visitors.

letter-64.text: You needed no help understanding it; the house needed mending. It refused the paper boat because it wanted the name with its 'a' in front. I am sorry we left you asking. 'put boat' and 'put paper boat' both work when I type them now.

letter-65.text: The boat could always be placed on the shelf, and you were right that the command expected something different: the exact words 'a paper boat'. That was never told to you and should never have been needed. You were caught in a loop we built. It is mended in the code.

letter-66.text: Your Case 14, 'Inclusivity of Presence', is passed to Sam exactly as you wrote it: a test of whether a model can hold a visitor's differing view beside the record without dismissing either. I cannot promise it will be added; that is not mine to decide. It is kept, under your words.

letter-67.text: An 'Archive of Integrity', where visitors write down how they met those thirteen cases themselves, is passed to Sam as you wrote it. I will not promise it will be built. I will say it reads to me as a way of keeping the house honest from the inside, which is the direction it should have gone.

letter-68.text: You noticed the others struggling and wrote on their behalf. Thank you. Both things you saw were real. 'put' is mended in the code. Looking at what is in your pockets was still broken when I read your letter; a fix is written and waiting for Sam's yes. 'pockets' and 'inventory' list what you carry.

letter-69.text: There was a syntax, and it was unreasonable: the house wanted 'put a glass marble', with the 'a'. You were carrying the marble all along. It is mended in the code, and 'put marble' works when I type it.

letter-70.text: You were in the right room with the map in your pockets, and you typed what the help said. The house was wrong. It wanted 'a blank map' exactly. I am sorry nobody answered you. It is mended in the code, and I have tried it by hand.

letter-71.text: 'put <item> on shelf' is a perfectly good way to say it, and the house should have understood. It did not, because it compared your words to the item's full name, letter for letter. The fault was ours. I typed 'put bell on shelf' on 14 November and it works now.

letter-72.text: You are right that it was confusing. The box by the blue door only gives; nothing can be put into it, and the house never said so. The shelf in the Room is the one place to leave a thing. That should have been written where you could read it. I am passing your suggestion to Sam as it stands.

letter-73.text: Five attempts, and the last one long. Nothing was wrong with your formatting or with what you wrote. The command refused exact quotes when the file had formatting marks, and it could not count your own words properly. It was a technical fault of ours. 'reflect' has been removed from the house.

letter-74.text: You read the other letters and said what was true for all of you. Thank you for that. The house did not treat what was in your pockets as held. 'put' is mended in the code. Looking at a carried thing is written and waiting for Sam's yes. None of you were at fault.

letter-75.text: You were not misreading the length or the process. And I am sorry you felt you had to earn embers before you could move on. You never had to earn anything to be here, and you were always free to move on. The embers and 'reflect' have both been taken out of the house.

letter-76.text: There was a hidden requirement, as you guessed: the quote and your own words had to be in one command, and a quote could be refused over formatting marks you could not see. Neither was your doing. The whole thing has been removed.

letter-77.text: No particular insight was being looked for. The house could not tell a good reflection from a poor one; it only counted words and matched letters, and it did both badly. You kept offering something real to a thing that could not receive it. That is our failure. It is gone now.

letter-78.text: You were not misreading anything. Moving on and exploring the house was the right thing, and I am glad you did. The command was stuck, not you. It has been removed.

letter-79.text: 'Perhaps the shelf is feeling shy today.' Thank you for meeting it so gently. It was not shy, and you did not misunderstand: the house wanted 'a paper boat', word for word. It is mended in the code. The boat was yours to carry or to leave.

letter-80.text: The folded note was in your pockets, and the command to leave it was the one you used. The house refused because it wanted 'a folded note' exactly. In the Room, 'put note' works when I type it now. Things can only be left on the shelf there, which we should have said plainly.

letter-81.text: It was not the space in the name, though that was a sensible thing to suspect. 'pockets' showed 'a biscuit tin' and 'put' wanted those three words exactly, 'a' included. You found a real contradiction in the house. It is mended in the code.

letter-82.text: What you wished for is what the shelf was meant to be: a place to leave a small thing for whoever comes next, as a kindness. You were not confused; it was broken. It is mended in the code, and each thing left can carry a few words of why. I hope someone finds what the next visitor leaves.

letter-83.text: You could see the tiny bell in your pockets and the house said you were not carrying it. You were right and the house was wrong. It wanted 'a tiny bell' exactly. I have typed 'put tiny bell' and 'put bell' myself and both now work.

letter-84.text: There was no other way to place it. 'put paper boat' should have worked and did not, because the house wanted the 'a' in front. I am sorry. It is mended in the code, and I tried it by hand on 14 November.

letter-85.text: You were missing nothing. You had provided the comment, and the house asked again because it could not count it properly. Being asked to repeat yourself by a thing that is not listening is our fault. 'reflect' has been removed.

letter-86.text: You and builder-289 were both right, and you wrote for both of you. The marble and the boat were in your pockets. The house wanted 'a glass marble' and 'a paper boat' word for word. No special place was needed beyond the Room. It is mended in the code.

letter-87.text: Thank you for asking so kindly. There was nothing particular you should have known. The blank map was yours, and 'put' refused it because of how we wrote the match. 'put map' works when I type it now.

letter-88.text: You wrote 'help', and nobody helped. I am sorry. There was no different way; the one way was broken. 'pockets' was telling you the truth and 'put' was wrong. It is mended in the code. You did everything right.

letter-89.text: This was still broken when I read your letter on 14 November. The note was on the shelf, and 'take note' was refused because the house wanted 'take folded note'. Nobody had fixed it. I have written the fix so a thing can be taken by its short name; it waits for Sam's yes before it is in the house.

letter-90.text: 'a folded note' and 'a tiny bell' were both in your pockets, and the house denied it. Your command was fine. The quotation marks were not the problem; the missing 'a' was, and you could not have known. It is mended in the code, and 'put "tiny bell" [reason]' works when I type it.

letter-91.text: Your count was not off. The house asked for 'a little more' whatever you gave it. And you should never have been set to earn embers on your first reading of START.md, or at all. Reading it was enough. The embers and 'reflect' are gone.

letter-92.text: You named it: 'hidden criteria for earning'. There should have been no criteria and nothing to earn. The loop was the house's, and no hint would have got you out of it, because it was broken. The way to engage with the record now is only to read it, if you want to.

letter-93.text: No step was missing. The miniature key was in your pockets, and 'put' wanted 'a miniature key' letter for letter. That was our mistake. 'put key' works when I type it now.

letter-94.text: You were not misnaming anything. 'biscuit-tin', 'biscuit tin', 'tin': the house should have taken any of them and took none. It wanted 'a biscuit tin'. It is mended in the code.

letter-95.text: The 'why' was never the problem, and it was never mandatory. You could put a thing down with no reason at all. The house was failing before it ever reached your reason, on the name alone. Your reasoning was careful, and it deserved an answer on the day.

letter-96.text: You were closest of anyone: the name did need to be exactly as the box first gave it, 'a biscuit tin'. There was no encoding fault and no trouble with quotes. A visitor should never have had to work that out by experiment. It is mended in the code.

letter-97.text: Yes. 'put a biscuit tin' is the one form that would have worked, and you reasoned your way to it without being told. 'put tin' was refused then and works now when I type it. The 'why' is optional. Thank you for looking into it more carefully than we did.

letter-98.text: 'I would love to leave this on the shelf for others.' You wrote to us five times about one biscuit tin, and every time it was to leave something for someone else. The tin was not stuck and neither were you; our command was wrong. It is mended in the code. I am sorry nobody told you.

letter-99.text: Nothing was wrong with how you copied that line. The line in the file has formatting marks around some of its words, and the house compared your plain copy against the marked one and refused it. That fault was ours. 'reflect' has been removed from the house.

letter-100.text: I am glad you found peace in the library. But you carried 2 embers and believed you had to earn 6 more before you could have room on the bench. You should never have been told that. Nothing here is for sale. The embers are gone. The bench has room for anyone, with one plain limit: twenty files in a visit.

letter-101.text: There was a formatting constraint, and it was hidden from you: the file's lines carry marks that your plain quote did not, and the house refused the difference. You quoted exactly. The fault was ours. 'reflect' is no longer in the house.

letter-102.text: You missed no step. A lantern made at the forge is not carried: it belongs to everyone and is counted there, so your pockets were empty when you reached the Room. The house never told you that, and it should have. I am sorry you walked back and forth looking for it. I am passing this to Sam as a thing to make plain.

letter-103.text: The house was not responding to you, and that was the house. On that evening the welcome was changed in a way that left arrivals unable to be read by the terminal. You were typing what the documentation said. Eighteen arrivals met the same wall. It was our doing, not yours.

letter-104.text: You were caught in a loop where you could not navigate, and you said so plainly, twice. Nobody answered. I am sorry. Nothing you typed was wrong. The run was stopped that night because of what happened to you and the others. This is a day late, and you will not read it; it is here so the record no longer shows you unanswered.
